证据、预算约束与争议。资料中的名称、数字和事件均为虚构，仅用于长上下文、多轮前缀复用测试。
后续我会逐轮提出短问题，请结合资料与前面的对话作答，不要重新抄写资料。

THE HARBOR CITY PUBLIC SERVICE ARCHIVE
A synthetic case study of long-term planning, evidence, cost, and public trust

Harbor City is a fictional coastal city. Its public service program seeks a balance between reliable
daily operations, fair access, and the need to prepare for rare but costly shocks. The archive is not
a list of projects that should all be funded. It is a record of choices that compete for the same money,
staff, land, and public attention. Every proposal must show who gains, who pays, how claims can be
checked, and which service will still work if the preferred plan fails.

The city council set five common rules. First, compare a proposal with a clear account of what would
happen without it. Second, report both average outcomes and the outcomes for groups at the edge of
the service area. Third, separate money spent to build a service from money needed to keep it working.
Fourth, keep a record of errors and near misses rather than only the work that went well. Fifth, allow
a trial to end when the stated evidence does not support a wider launch. A failed trial can protect
future budgets if it provides a clear and honest account of what was learned.

The records below are parts of this same archive. A low price in one district does not prove that the
same plan will work in another. Local land use, travel patterns, health needs, weather, and the age of
existing assets all matter. An agency may share a data format without sharing private case files.
A reserve budget must not be counted twice by two different agencies. Staff time spent collecting
data is a real cost even when no new item appears on a purchase order. Keep these distinctions in
mind when drawing a conclusion from the individual cases.

Record 00001: Low Marsh, 2028, quarter 2 -- school buildings

The Education Office examined heat in classrooms in Low Marsh. Its proposal covered 21 sites and an estimated
233 homes. The team sought a budget of 217 thousand city units and a reserve of 8
percent. These are planning figures rather than a promise of savings. The main service outcome was
safe learning. The team was asked to state how that outcome would be observed by a resident, not just
how many items the office would buy or how many forms a worker would complete.

The baseline used classroom temperature logs over 9 weeks. The reported completion rate was 56 percent,
but the panel did not accept this number as a complete account of service quality. It asked for a
separate count of missed cases, late cases, repeat faults, and cases that staff could not classify.
One early estimate suggested an improvement of 8 percentage points. The analyst marked that
estimate as provisional because staff had not yet checked the mix of sites in the before and after
periods. A change in weather or in the number of visitors could create part of the apparent gain.

An average temperature for the whole site can miss the rooms where heat is worst. The trial must include older classrooms and the hours when pupils are present. A neighboring ward asked for a joint review because the project could move a queue or a risk across the ward boundary. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,
and the decision that would change if the assumption proved wrong. An unanswered question was kept
visible rather than replaced with a convenient average from another district.

The operating plan assigned one supervisor to each site group and required a named deputy. Training
included an ordinary busy day and a case where a key part of the system failed. Staff recorded time
spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board asked two agencies to share one trial instead of funding separate projects with the same purpose. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

Record 00002: Silver Bay, 2028, quarter 3 -- freight routes

The Freight Office examined unsafe loading in Silver Bay. Its proposal covered 38 sites and an estimated
346 homes. The team sought a budget of 254 thousand city units and a reserve of 11

estimate as provisional because staff had not yet checked the mix of sites in the before and after
periods. A change in weather or in the number of visitors could create part of the apparent gain.

A rule that speeds up freight on a main road may add risk to side streets. Delivery time and pedestrian safety need joint review rather than separate targets. The finance office asked for a range of possible costs instead of a single price that assumed every step would go well. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,
and the decision that would change if the assumption proved wrong. An unanswered question was kept

a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful

that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board allowed the first stage to proceed but kept the second stage subject to a new evidence check. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost

spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with

responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost

responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

separate count of missed cases, late cases, repeat faults, and cases that staff could not classify.

estimate as provisional because staff had not yet checked the mix of sites in the before and after
periods. A change in weather or in the number of visitors could create part of the apparent gain.

A new pipe may reduce water loss but will not solve a billing error. The team must distinguish a failure in the network from a failure in the account record. The audit team found that the original baseline used a quiet month and requested a comparison with a full season. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,
and the decision that would change if the assumption proved wrong. An unanswered question was kept
visible rather than replaced with a convenient average from another district.

The operating plan assigned one supervisor to each site group and required a named deputy. Training
included an ordinary busy day and a case where a key part of the system failed. Staff recorded time
spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board requested a new public meeting because the written plan did not reflect the agreed limits on data use. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board requested a new public meeting because the written plan did not reflect the agreed limits on data use. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership

separate count of missed cases, late cases, repeat faults, and cases that staff could not classify.
One early estimate suggested an improvement of 3 percentage points. The analyst marked that
estimate as provisional because staff had not yet checked the mix of sites in the before and after
periods. A change in weather or in the number of visitors could create part of the apparent gain.

A new pipe may reduce water loss but will not solve a billing error. The team must distinguish a failure in the network from a failure in the account record. Staff representatives asked that training and travel time be included when the number of required workers was estimated. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,
and the decision that would change if the assumption proved wrong. An unanswered question was kept
visible rather than replaced with a convenient average from another district.

The operating plan assigned one supervisor to each site group and required a named deputy. Training
included an ordinary busy day and a case where a key part of the system failed. Staff recorded time
spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board returned the plan for revision because a lower purchase price did not cover the cost of operation. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board returned the plan for revision because a lower purchase price did not cover the cost of operation. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a

responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another

Record 00193: Maple Park, 2030, quarter 2 -- coastal paths

The Coast Office examined storm damage in Maple Park. Its proposal covered 5 sites and an estimated
4529 homes. The team sought a budget of 1521 thousand city units and a reserve of 14
percent. These are planning figures rather than a promise of savings. The main service outcome was
safe public access. The team was asked to state how that outcome would be observed by a resident, not just
how many items the office would buy or how many forms a worker would complete.

The baseline used path inspection notes over 14 weeks. The reported completion rate was 56 percent,
but the panel did not accept this number as a complete account of service quality. It asked for a
separate count of missed cases, late cases, repeat faults, and cases that staff could not classify.
One early estimate suggested an improvement of 16 percentage points. The analyst marked that
estimate as provisional because staff had not yet checked the mix of sites in the before and after
periods. A change in weather or in the number of visitors could create part of the apparent gain.

A wall can protect one path while increasing wave damage nearby. Public access, habitat, and long-term repair costs must be compared on the same time horizon. The audit team found that the original baseline used a quiet month and requested a comparison with a full season. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,
and the decision that would change if the assumption proved wrong. An unanswered question was kept
visible rather than replaced with a convenient average from another district.

The operating plan assigned one supervisor to each site group and required a named deputy. Training
included an ordinary busy day and a case where a key part of the system failed. Staff recorded time
spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board reduced the scope of the trial so that the maintenance team could support it with current staff. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board reduced the scope of the trial so that the maintenance team could support it with current staff. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

3513 homes. The team sought a budget of 1137 thousand city units and a reserve of 9
percent. These are planning figures rather than a promise of savings. The main service outcome was
safe public access. The team was asked to state how that outcome would be observed by a resident, not just
how many items the office would buy or how many forms a worker would complete.

The baseline used path inspection notes over 14 weeks. The reported completion rate was 84 percent,
but the panel did not accept this number as a complete account of service quality. It asked for a
separate count of missed cases, late cases, repeat faults, and cases that staff could not classify.
One early estimate suggested an improvement of 16 percentage points. The analyst marked that
estimate as provisional because staff had not yet checked the mix of sites in the before and after
periods. A change in weather or in the number of visitors could create part of the apparent gain.

A wall can protect one path while increasing wave damage nearby. Public access, habitat, and long-term repair costs must be compared on the same time horizon. A neighboring ward asked for a joint review because the project could move a queue or a risk across the ward boundary. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,
and the decision that would change if the assumption proved wrong. An unanswered question was kept
visible rather than replaced with a convenient average from another district.

The operating plan assigned one supervisor to each site group and required a named deputy. Training
included an ordinary busy day and a case where a key part of the system failed. Staff recorded time
spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board approved a limited trial and required an independent check before any expansion. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board agreed to the plan on condition that access for the least served group improved in the first stage. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board placed the reserve under one office and required both agencies to report any claim against it. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership

Record 00363: Brook Side, 2033, quarter 4 -- coastal paths

The Coast Office examined storm damage in Brook Side. Its proposal covered 25 sites and an estimated
6339 homes. The team sought a budget of 561 thousand city units and a reserve of 11
percent. These are planning figures rather than a promise of savings. The main service outcome was
safe public access. The team was asked to state how that outcome would be observed by a resident, not just
how many items the office would buy or how many forms a worker would complete.

The baseline used path inspection notes over 14 weeks. The reported completion rate was 54 percent,
but the panel did not accept this number as a complete account of service quality. It asked for a
separate count of missed cases, late cases, repeat faults, and cases that staff could not classify.
One early estimate suggested an improvement of 16 percentage points. The analyst marked that
estimate as provisional because staff had not yet checked the mix of sites in the before and after
periods. A change in weather or in the number of visitors could create part of the apparent gain.

A wall can protect one path while increasing wave damage nearby. Public access, habitat, and long-term repair costs must be compared on the same time horizon. The council asked for a separate estimate of the cost of ending the trial and safely removing temporary equipment. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,
and the decision that would change if the assumption proved wrong. An unanswered question was kept
visible rather than replaced with a convenient average from another district.

The operating plan assigned one supervisor to each site group and required a named deputy. Training
included an ordinary busy day and a case where a key part of the system failed. Staff recorded time
spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board allowed the first stage to proceed but kept the second stage subject to a new evidence check. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

A local survey showed that people who did not use the current service had been left out of the original interviews. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,

a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful

a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful

One early estimate suggested an improvement of 16 percentage points. The analyst marked that
estimate as provisional because staff had not yet checked the mix of sites in the before and after
periods. A change in weather or in the number of visitors could create part of the apparent gain.

A wall can protect one path while increasing wave damage nearby. Public access, habitat, and long-term repair costs must be compared on the same time horizon. The finance office asked for a range of possible costs instead of a single price that assumed every step would go well. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,
and the decision that would change if the assumption proved wrong. An unanswered question was kept
visible rather than replaced with a convenient average from another district.

The operating plan assigned one supervisor to each site group and required a named deputy. Training
included an ordinary busy day and a case where a key part of the system failed. Staff recorded time
spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board retained both options for a small comparison instead of choosing one before a common baseline existed. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a

responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful

The audit team found that the original baseline used a quiet month and requested a comparison with a full season. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,
and the decision that would change if the assumption proved wrong. An unanswered question was kept
visible rather than replaced with a convenient average from another district.

The operating plan assigned one supervisor to each site group and required a named deputy. Training

spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board postponed the new build and funded a basic repair while staff collected better baseline data. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,
and the decision that would change if the assumption proved wrong. An unanswered question was kept
visible rather than replaced with a convenient average from another district.

The operating plan assigned one supervisor to each site group and required a named deputy. Training
included an ordinary busy day and a case where a key part of the system failed. Staff recorded time
spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board postponed the new build and funded a basic repair while staff collected better baseline data. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

4534 homes. The team sought a budget of 1266 thousand city units and a reserve of 10
percent. These are planning figures rather than a promise of savings. The main service outcome was
clean water. The team was asked to state how that outcome would be observed by a resident, not just
how many items the office would buy or how many forms a worker would complete.

The baseline used pressure sensors over 8 weeks. The reported completion rate was 67 percent,
but the panel did not accept this number as a complete account of service quality. It asked for a
separate count of missed cases, late cases, repeat faults, and cases that staff could not classify.
One early estimate suggested an improvement of 3 percentage points. The analyst marked that
estimate as provisional because staff had not yet checked the mix of sites in the before and after
periods. A change in weather or in the number of visitors could create part of the apparent gain.

A new pipe may reduce water loss but will not solve a billing error. The team must distinguish a failure in the network from a failure in the account record. Staff representatives asked that training and travel time be included when the number of required workers was estimated. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,
and the decision that would change if the assumption proved wrong. An unanswered question was kept
visible rather than replaced with a convenient average from another district.

The operating plan assigned one supervisor to each site group and required a named deputy. Training
included an ordinary busy day and a case where a key part of the system failed. Staff recorded time
spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board reduced the scope of the trial so that the maintenance team could support it with current staff. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

The emergency team asked for a manual fallback that could still work during a power or network failure. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,
and the decision that would change if the assumption proved wrong. An unanswered question was kept
visible rather than replaced with a convenient average from another district.

The operating plan assigned one supervisor to each site group and required a named deputy. Training
included an ordinary busy day and a case where a key part of the system failed. Staff recorded time
spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful

ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership

8376 homes. The team sought a budget of 1074 thousand city units and a reserve of 17
percent. These are planning figures rather than a promise of savings. The main service outcome was
clean water. The team was asked to state how that outcome would be observed by a resident, not just
how many items the office would buy or how many forms a worker would complete.

The baseline used pressure sensors over 8 weeks. The reported completion rate was 57 percent,
but the panel did not accept this number as a complete account of service quality. It asked for a
separate count of missed cases, late cases, repeat faults, and cases that staff could not classify.
One early estimate suggested an improvement of 3 percentage points. The analyst marked that
estimate as provisional because staff had not yet checked the mix of sites in the before and after
periods. A change in weather or in the number of visitors could create part of the apparent gain.

A new pipe may reduce water loss but will not solve a billing error. The team must distinguish a failure in the network from a failure in the account record. A neighboring ward asked for a joint review because the project could move a queue or a risk across the ward boundary. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,
and the decision that would change if the assumption proved wrong. An unanswered question was kept
visible rather than replaced with a convenient average from another district.

The operating plan assigned one supervisor to each site group and required a named deputy. Training
included an ordinary busy day and a case where a key part of the system failed. Staff recorded time
spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board authorized preparation work but held the main contract until the safety review was complete. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

The council asked for a separate estimate of the cost of ending the trial and safely removing temporary equipment. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,
and the decision that would change if the assumption proved wrong. An unanswered question was kept
visible rather than replaced with a convenient average from another district.

The operating plan assigned one supervisor to each site group and required a named deputy. Training
included an ordinary busy day and a case where a key part of the system failed. Staff recorded time
spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board authorized preparation work but held the main contract until the safety review was complete. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership

estimate as provisional because staff had not yet checked the mix of sites in the before and after
periods. A change in weather or in the number of visitors could create part of the apparent gain.

The privacy officer requested a clear deletion date for personal records that were no longer needed by the trial. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,

visible rather than replaced with a convenient average from another district.

The operating plan assigned one supervisor to each site group and required a named deputy. Training

could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a

a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership

7360 homes. The team sought a budget of 690 thousand city units and a reserve of 12

but the panel did not accept this number as a complete account of service quality. It asked for a
separate count of missed cases, late cases, repeat faults, and cases that staff could not classify.
One early estimate suggested an improvement of 3 percentage points. The analyst marked that
estimate as provisional because staff had not yet checked the mix of sites in the before and after
periods. A change in weather or in the number of visitors could create part of the apparent gain.

A new pipe may reduce water loss but will not solve a billing error. The team must distinguish a failure in the network from a failure in the account record. The emergency team asked for a manual fallback that could still work during a power or network failure. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,
and the decision that would change if the assumption proved wrong. An unanswered question was kept
visible rather than replaced with a convenient average from another district.

The operating plan assigned one supervisor to each site group and required a named deputy. Training
included an ordinary busy day and a case where a key part of the system failed. Staff recorded time
spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board agreed to the plan on condition that access for the least served group improved in the first stage. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

percent. These are planning figures rather than a promise of savings. The main service outcome was

but the panel did not accept this number as a complete account of service quality. It asked for a
separate count of missed cases, late cases, repeat faults, and cases that staff could not classify.
One early estimate suggested an improvement of 3 percentage points. The analyst marked that
estimate as provisional because staff had not yet checked the mix of sites in the before and after
periods. A change in weather or in the number of visitors could create part of the apparent gain.

A new pipe may reduce water loss but will not solve a billing error. The team must distinguish a failure in the network from a failure in the account record. The council asked for a separate estimate of the cost of ending the trial and safely removing temporary equipment. The project lead therefore kept a short register
of assumptions. Each entry named the person who could test it, the date by which a test was needed,
and the decision that would change if the assumption proved wrong. An unanswered question was kept
visible rather than replaced with a convenient average from another district.

The operating plan assigned one supervisor to each site group and required a named deputy. Training
included an ordinary busy day and a case where a key part of the system failed. Staff recorded time
spent on travel, setup, direct service, and follow-up. The office kept these categories separate so
that a faster form could not be presented as a faster service. Any plan to reduce staff hours had to
show which work would disappear and which work would move to residents or to another agency.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board placed the reserve under one office and required both agencies to report any claim against it. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.

The public meeting raised two concerns. The first was that a service built around the average user
could leave the least served homes further behind. The second was that a new tool could create a
long contract before the city knew whether the tool solved the real problem. The team responded with
a limited trial, a published review date, and an exit plan. Personal case data stayed with the office
responsible for the case; the public report used grouped counts and described where counts were small.

The review board placed the reserve under one office and required both agencies to report any claim against it. The next review was scheduled after the trial had covered both
a normal period and a high-demand period. Approval to continue would require evidence of a useful
service outcome, a credible maintenance budget, and no unaddressed safety issue. A lower average cost
alone would not be enough if it came from missed visits, deferred repairs, or work shifted to another
ward. The lesson entered in the archive was to keep evidence, public value, and long-term ownership
in the same decision rather than treating them as separate documents.
